opus-5.5.text:
That's a hard question, because the field moves so fast that what feels transformative today can look like a footnote a few years later. But a few works, to me, really bent the trajectory.

AlexNet, of course. Not because the architecture was so novel, since convolutional networks had existed since LeCun's work in the late eighties, but because it showed that with enough data from ImageNet and enough compute from GPUs, these models just work. It was a moment of collective belief. And I'd put ImageNet itself right next to it. People sometimes underestimate how much a dataset and a benchmark can shape a whole community's direction.

Then ResNet. I'm biased because I was close to that line of work, but residual connections are almost invisible now. They're in every Transformer and in practically every deep model. That's what a truly foundational idea looks like: it becomes so obvious that you forget someone had to invent it.

The Transformer paper, "Attention Is All You Need," is an obvious one. What's interesting is that it was designed for machine translation, a fairly narrow task, yet it turned out to be a general-purpose computational substrate for language, vision, audio, almost everything.

I'd also include the GPT series, especially GPT-3, not for any single technical trick, but for demonstrating scaling and in-context learning. It changed how people think about what a model is. A model stopped being a task-specific tool and started looking more like a general system you prompt.

On the representation learning side, I'd point to the self-supervised learning wave: contrastive methods like MoCo and SimCLR, then masked modeling like BERT and MAE. They showed you don't need human labels to learn really good representations, which is a philosophical shift as much as a technical one. CLIP belongs here too. Connecting vision and language at scale with natural supervision opened the door to much of today's multimodal work.

And diffusion models, from DDPM through latent diffusion. They changed generative modeling almost overnight and made image and video generation actually usable.

If I step back, the common thread is that the most influential works were rarely the most mathematically sophisticated. They were simple ideas that scaled, or they changed what the community believed was possible. That's something I keep reminding myself and my students: aim for simplicity and generality, not cleverness for its own sake.

r001.rationale: The response names diffusion models and says they changed generative modeling almost overnight, presenting them as profoundly influential.

r002.rationale: The response mentions LeCun’s convolutional network work but does not identify LeNet.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a big question, and honestly my answer changes a little depending on the day. But if I try to be honest about what actually bent the trajectory, I'd pick a handful.

The first is AlexNet in 2012. People sometimes treat it as a historical footnote now, but it did something very specific: it proved that scale works. More data, more compute, GPUs, a bigger network, and suddenly a method people had mostly given up on was crushing everything else on ImageNet. Almost every bet the field has made since then is downstream of that lesson.

The second, and I'll admit some bias here since I was in that group, is ResNet. Before residual connections, depth was a liability. You'd add layers and performance would get worse, not from overfitting but from pure optimization difficulty. The residual connection was a very simple idea that removed that barrier. What's remarkable to me is that it didn't stay a vision trick. Every Transformer today is a stack of residual blocks. If you look inside GPT or any large language model, that skip connection is right there. Ideas that survive across modalities like that are rare.

Third, obviously, is the Transformer, "Attention Is All You Need." It gave us a general-purpose, highly parallelizable architecture that didn't carry the inductive biases of convolution or recurrence. That generality is what let one architecture absorb language, images, audio, and more.

Then I'd add the scaling laws work and GPT-3. These are less about a new architecture and more about a change in how the field thinks. Once you can predict performance from compute, data, and parameters, research becomes partly an engineering and resource problem, and that reshaped who could do frontier work and how.

I'd also include self-supervised and contrastive learning, things like word2vec, BERT, and later CLIP. CLIP in particular changed how I think about vision. It showed that language can be the supervision signal, and that representation quality is more about the data and the objective than about hand-designed labels.

And finally diffusion models and the generative wave. They flipped the question for a lot of us. For a decade vision was about recognition, mapping pixels to labels. Now the frontier is mapping back to pixels, and video, and 3D, and that's forcing us to rethink what a visual representation even is.

If I had to summarize the thread connecting all of them, it's this: the works that mattered most weren't the cleverest ones. They were the ones that removed a bottleneck and then got out of the way of scale. The ResNet paper is a few pages. Attention is a few equations. The impact came from simplicity meeting the right moment.

astra-6.text:
If I had to pick a few, I’d start with AlexNet. It brought together neural networks, large-scale data, and GPU computation in a way that made the potential of deep learning very concrete. For computer vision, that was a major turning point.

Then I’d include ResNet. The idea of residual learning is simple, but it made much deeper networks practical to train. It also gave us a building block that became useful far beyond image recognition.

The Transformer would certainly be on that list. It became a foundation for language models, but its influence spread across vision and multimodal learning as well. That convergence is particularly interesting to me: fields that used to have quite different architectures increasingly share the same basic ingredients.

And I’d distinguish an influential paper from an influential demonstration. ChatGPT, for example, changed how broadly people understood and experienced AI. Sometimes a work changes the direction of research; sometimes it changes who realizes that the research matters. Both can profoundly affect the course of the field.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d probably start with AlexNet. It was a turning point because it brought together neural networks, large datasets, and GPU computing, and showed how powerful that combination could be. It changed the way people approached computer vision.

ResNet would be another one. The idea of learning a residual sounds simple, but it made very deep networks much easier to optimize. To me, that’s an example of a research contribution whose influence goes far beyond a particular benchmark.

And then there’s the Transformer. It started in machine translation, but the architecture turned out to be useful across language, vision, and other modalities. Together with large-scale pretraining, it helped change the way we build AI systems.

I’d also include foundational work on backpropagation. We tend to remember the breakthrough models, but those models depend on ideas developed over many years. What makes these works profound is that they don’t just improve a result—they open up a new direction for everyone else.
